title: Lab 2: Investigating claims using inference
text:
Investigating “yes/no” questions with permutation
Let’s investigate the claim “Lead is elevated in the drip line compared to the rest of the yard” as a yes/no question.

State your hypotheses
Recall that it is more straightforward to find evidence against a hypothesis than for it. So when we investigate yes/no questions, we set up a null hypothesis and see how much evidence there is against it.
State the null and alternative hypotheses for this claim.
\(H_0\):
\(H_A\):


Calculate the observed value of the statistic
We’ll use the difference in means between samples from the drip line and the yard as the statistic for this question.






Important



Remember, the mean isn’t always the most appropriate statistic for representing a distribution! Always think critically about how your data relates to the question.


Calculate the difference in means between the drip line and yard observations in the sample. Remember, this should be a single number (not a data frame or pair of means).


Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic
This statistical experiment simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) just due to chance alone. To conduct this experiment, we have to break the connection between the predictor variable (location code) and response (lead concentration). Randomizing the predictor leaves the variation in the response untouched, while removing any assocation between the two.
Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic. Do it just once - we’ll repeat in the next section.






Tip



sample() can be used to shuffle vectors.




Repeat shuffling
In the previous section, you simulated one statistic from the null hypothesis. What we need now is a whole bunch of statistics from the null hypothesis - our null distribution.
Repeat shuffling 10,000 times to create a vector that simulates the null distribution.






Tip



replicate() repeatedly runs expressions over and over.


Visualize the null distribution using a histogram.


Compare the observed to the null
The previous figure showed the expected distribution of the statistic (the difference in mean lead between drip line and yard) under the null hypothesis. How does that compare to the observed value?
Plot the null distribution again, but this time add a vertical line indicating the observed statistic.
Calculate your p-value.






Note



A p-value is the probability of observing the sample (or something more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true.




Interpret your results
Based on your p-value, do you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?

title: Lab 2: Investigating claims using inference
text:
Investigating “how much?” questions with bootstrapping
Now, let’s investigate the claim “Neighborhoods north of the Exide plant were exposed to more lead than those south” as a how much? question.

Calculate the observed value of the statistic
Once again, let’s use the difference in means as our statistic. Calculate the difference in means between properties in the extended north area and those in the extended south area.






Tip



Use dplyr functions to wrangle the soil core data for this part. Properties starting with “ENA” are in the extended north area, and the “ESA” prefix means extended south area. str_sub() will help here.




Resample observations and recalculate the statistic
Bootstrapping simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) from sampling. Compare this to permutation, which is about variation just due to chance. For this experiment, we will assume the sample is representative of the population and repeatedly draw “new” samples. This process simulates the process of collecting new samples.
Resample rows from the data frame and recalculate the statistic. Repeat this 10,000 times to simulate the sampling distribution.






Tip



Use slice_sample() with replacement to get bootstrap samples.


Visualize the sampling distribution using a histogram.


Find the confidence interval
The previous figure showed how your statistic varies due to slight differences between samples. Use this sampling distribution to estimate the 95% confidence interval.






Note



A confidence interval is a range of values that you are confident contains the population parameter.








Tip



Use the quantile() function to find the middle 95% of the sampling distribution.


Plot the sampling distribution again, but this time add vertical lines indicating the observed statistic and the 95% CI.


Interpret your results
Based on your confidence interval, how much could the difference in lead exposure between north and south be?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?

Done early? Having fun and want more? Try this out.
P-values are sensitive to sample sizes. Do the permutation exercise again, but this time only on a sub-sample of the data. What kinds of p-values do you get if you only use 20 observations? 50? 100? 1000? title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Between November 2013 and July 2015, contractors working under the oversight of the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) sampled soil lead concentrations at hundreds of residential properties near the former Exide Technologies battery recycling facility in Vernon, CA. Crews collected soil cores from several locations on each property and analyzed them in a laboratory for lead content. This sampling campaign, and this lab’s data, are described in the DTSC Preliminary Estimate of the Geographical Boundary of Emissions report (Department of Toxic Substances Control 2015).
A single soil sample is a measurement of a property’s soil lead level, but no single measurement perfectly captures the “true” lead burden of an entire property. In this lab you’ll explore how much soil lead measurements vary within a property, and how that variability depends on where on the property a sample was taken. This is a question about reliability: if you sampled the same property twice, how close would the two measurements be?

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Between November 2013 and July 2015, contractors working under the oversight of the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) sampled soil lead concentrations at hundreds of residential properties near the former Exide Technologies battery recycling facility in Vernon, CA. Crews collected soil cores from several locations on each property and analyzed them in a laboratory for lead content. This sampling campaign, and this lab’s data, are described in the DTSC Preliminary Estimate of the Geographical Boundary of Emissions report (Department of Toxic Substances Control 2015).
A single soil sample is a measurement of a property’s soil lead level, but no single measurement perfectly captures the “true” lead burden of an entire property. In this lab you’ll explore how much soil lead measurements vary within a property, and how that variability depends on where on the property a sample was taken. This is a question about reliability: if you sampled the same property twice, how close would the two measurements be?

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
The data
exide-soil-cores.csv contains a subset of the DTSC’s public data table for the Exide site. You can find it on Workbench under /courses/EDS222/data. It’s limited to the samples collected during the initial and expanded assessments in 2013-2015. The full DTSC public data table contains lots more - you are encouraged to explore it further!

Data dictionary







Column
Description




property_id
Identifier for the property a sample was collected from.


sample_id
Identifier for an individual soil sample (boring).


sample_date
Date the sample was collected.


location_code
Where on the property the sample was taken. DL = drip line. YD = yard.


pb_ppm
Lead concentration, in parts per million (ppm).


longitude, latitude
Coordinates of the property (WGS84).





What does a row represent?
Each row is one soil core collected from one location on one property, at a depth of 3 inches below ground surface. Properties were sampled at multiple locations, so property_id repeats across rows: a single property typically contributes up to ten yard samples and a handful of drip line samples.


What’s a drip line?
The drip line is the narrow strip of soil at the edge of a building’s roof - the line where rainwater drips or is directed off the roof and gutters. It sits right against the house, in contrast to the rest of the yard, the more open part of the property further from the building. Because paint (a historical source of lead) tends to chip and weather off exterior walls, and because roof runoff concentrates atmospheric deposition falling on the roof into a narrow band, drip line soil can experience different pollutant exposure than yard soil.

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Lab activity

library(tidyverse)


1. Read in the data


2. Distribution of soil core lead measurements
Create a histogram to visualize the distribution of pb_ppm across all samples. How does it compare to the California (80 ppm) and EPA (200 ppm) thresholds for lead in residential soil?


3. Distribution of property-level mean measurements
Calculate the mean pb_ppm for each property. What’s the distribution of these property-level means? How does it compare to the distribution of individual soil cores from question 2?


4. Property-level variability
How variable are soil core lead measurements at the property level? Plot the distribution of property-level standard deviations of pb_ppm. What does your plot suggest about the reliability of soil lead measurements?


5. Lead measurements by location
What is the distribution of pb_ppm for drip line samples (location_code == "DL") versus everything else (the yard samples)? How much higher do drip line measurements appear to be relative to yard measurements?


6. Drip line vs. yard, at the property level
Part 5 looked at the aggregate distribution across all samples. Now let’s look at drip line vs. yard within each property.
a. Create a new column called is_dripline: a logical column that’s TRUE for drip line locations and FALSE otherwise.
b. Group the data by property and is_dripline, and calculate the mean soil lead concentration in each group.
c. For each property, calculate the difference between the mean drip line measurement and the mean non-drip-line (yard) measurement. Hint: pivoting will help!
d. Plot the distribution of the property-level drip line/yard differences.

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Interpretation
Interpret your final plot from the perspective of reliability. If you’re estimating the representative soil lead concentration for a property, how does sample location affect measurement reliability? What do you think you should do with the data from different locations?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical and parametric samples
Empirical: derived directly from observations
Parametric: derived from a mathematical formula governed by one or a few parameters

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical samples: random
The process of collecting real observations is how we get empirical samples.
When feasible, simple random samples are most representative of the population.

IMS Figure 2.1: a simple random sample of recent graduates.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical samples: biased
A truly random sample is rarely possible. Without care, there are many ways for biases to creep in. Convenience bias is particularly common.

IMS Figure 2.2: a biased sample.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical samples: stratified
Even if simple random sampling is infeasible, sampling strategies reduce bias. For example, stratified sampling divides the population into self-similar groups, then randomly samples within those groups.


IMS Figure 2.4: a stratified sample.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Example of a parametric distribution

Parametric distributions are defined by parameters (instead of observed data).

E.g., a normal distribution has two parameters - the mean controls location and the sd controls shape.

Recall probability density functions (PDFs) tell us how probable different ranges of values are.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Parameterizing a distribution
Let’s parameterize a normal distribution with the mean and sd of the lead soil dataset.

soil_cores |>
  summarize(
    mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm),
    sd_pb_ppm = sd(pb_ppm)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_pb_ppm sd_pb_ppm
        <dbl>     <dbl>
1        253.      371.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Probability density function

The PDF describes the relative probability of observing different values.
This PDF is a normal distribution with parameters matching the lead soil dataset.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
A universe of parametric distributions

The normal distribution is a poor stand-in for the lead data (symmetric, possibly negative).
A different family (e.g. the lognormal) could do a better job. We’ll cover these more in later weeks.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Sampling parametric distributions

We will sample from parametric distributions frequently in this course.
Think of the height of the PDF as the chance of observing a nearby value.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Empirical and parametric samples
Empirical: derived directly from observations.

E.g., lead concentrations in soil cores.

Parametric: derived from a mathematical formula governed by one or a few parameters.

E.g., a normal distribution with a mean and sd.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Sampling strategies

Simple random is most representative of the population, but often infeasible.
Sampling bias misleads inferences about the population.
Sampling strategies (e.g. stratification) work around biases.


IMS Figure 2.1: a simple random sample of recent graduates.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Parametric distributions

Parametric distributions are mathematical functions governed by parameters.
We use them as theoretical stand-ins for populations.
PDF says how probable observations are, given parameters.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Navigating uncertainty

If we could directly observe everything without error, we wouldn’t need statistics
In practice, we only get a glimpse through a window at what we care about
Statistics is the practice of interpreting data to understand the whole from the limited part we can see

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Challenges of statistical inference

Generalizing from sample to population
Generalizing from treatment to control group
Generalizing from observed measurements to underlying constructs of interest

(Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari 2021)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Neither math nor magic
Statistics uses math (just like any other field of science) but it’s not a type of math

Sure, calculus and linear algebra can be useful, but we’ll mostly bypass them
Instead, we will instead use simulation to develop (and test) conceptual models

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Neither math nor magic
To perform a statistical analysis responsibly you need to understand the assumptions and risks

Many applications of statistics … invoke statistical terms and procedures as incantations, with scant understanding of the assumptions or relevance of the calculations, or even the meaning of the terminology. This demotes statistics from a way of thinking about evidence and avoiding self-deception to a formal “blessing” of claims.

(Stark and Saltelli 2018)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
A way of thinking

In this class you will learn statistical thinking for assessing and interpreting evidence
We will avoid formulaic flowcharts for picking tests and models
The decisions and choices made by statistics practitioners have real world consequences

title: Final Project
text:
Most of the course material in EDS 222 focuses on a single case study: the Exide battery recycling plant. We will explore data to answer environmental data science questions using statistical thinking. In your final project, you will apply these same skills to a case study of your own choosing. Using real data and appropriate analyses, you will write a technical blog post investigating an environmental question.
Your technical blog post is a valuable contribution to your professional portfolio. The analysis in your project will demonstrate your competency in statistical thinking and tools. But on its own, an analysis has no impact. Just as importantly, your writing will show that you can think critically about questions and data, and communicate effectively about methods and interpretation.
In terms of complexity and detail, it should fall somewhere between a news article and peer-reviewed research. This article on Medium is a good representative. Just be aware that it uses some techniques you won’t see until EDS 241.

title: Final Project
text:
Rubric
Your final project will be assessed according to the following rubric.

Question and data (15%)
An analysis means nothing without context! Before you show off your technical aptitude, give your audience motivation to care about your question.
The blog post provides context and background for the question
The data are explained using text and figures
The theorized causal relationships are described with a DAG


Statistical model (35%)
It is often said, “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” Describe your modeling approach in sufficient detail to understand both its utility as well as its limitations.
The statistical model is explained conceptually and using formal statistical notation
The choice of model is justified based on the characteristics of the data and model assumptions
Potential limitations of the model and data are considered


Inference (35%)
Interpret your model in the context of your question and data. Remember that confidence intervals and p-values are tools for inference, not goals in of themselves. A robust interpretation of a non-significant result is far more compelling than a superficial treatment of a small p-value.
Hypotheses are stated in plain language and with visualizations
Model estimates are presented with appropriate uncertainty
A hypothesis is tested and the evidence is interpreted


Professionalism (15%)
Your portfolio pieces will feature in your future job applications. This final project is not just about a grade in a class, it’s a part of your job search. You’re going to put a lot of work into this project - let’s make sure hiring managers see the fruits of that labor.
The overall appearance of the blog post (e.g., figures, code outputs) is portfolio-quality
The writing is comprehensible to a technical audience
The project repository is well-organized and appropriately documented

title: Week 1 Wednesday pre-class
text:
So far this week, you’ve learned about:
The three challenges of statistics
Measurements and data
In class on Wednesday, we’ll discuss these concepts in the context of statistical claims on topics you’re interested in.

title: Week 1 Wednesday pre-class
text:
Instructions
Before class, find a statistical claim. Search the areas of environmental science you’re passionate and knowledgeable about. This could be in a news article, a YouTube video, a documentary, etc. It’s important that you find a claim that is presented as having statistical support.
Respond to the prompts in this Google Form about your claim.

title: Week 1 Wednesday pre-class
text:
Example
Describe the claim
Corals growing near islands with healthy seabird colonies grow more than twice as fast as corals near islands where invasive rats have wiped out the seabirds.
Where did you find it?
Audubon Magazine The Remarkable Healing Power of Seabird Poop for Climate-Stressed Coral Reefs
What challenge of statistics does it fall under?
Generalize from treatment to control. The “treatment” is the presence of invasive rats (which extirpate seabirds), the “control” is islands without rats.
Pick the most salient variable in the data. In what ways does it accurately represent what its meant to, and in what ways might it be different? (I.e., assess its validity.)
Coral growth rate. This was measured using the area of corals from photographs1. The claim about growth rate is really more about mass or volume, however area is a reasonably valid proxy because previous research has established area and mass are highly correlated.
Continuing with the same variable, what are the limitations on its reliability?
Estimates of area from photographs are sensitive to the angle of the photo and the judgement of the researcher who traces the photo. Although those factors can affect reliability, the study used photos from divers, which are more reliable than photos taken by aircraft or satellites.
Continuing with the same variable, how was the sample collected? Were there obstacles to selecting a representative sample?
The sample came from twelve islands in the Chagos Archipelago (six had rats, six didn’t). There is potential selection bias because this was an observational study, so the researchers couldn’t randomize which islands got rats and which didn’t. Also, the study only looked at one species of coral. It’s possible other corals are more or less affected by seabird abundance.

This information isn’t directly in the magazine article, but I’m familiar with the methods. This is why it’s important to pick a statistical claim in a scientific field you’re knowledgeable about!↩︎

title: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Course Description
Statistics is the science of collecting, manipulating, and analyzing empirical data. In this class, we will learn the statistical fundamentals that will enable us to draw conclusions about the environment and its interaction with social and economic systems. We will cover fundamental statistical concepts and tools, and then apply and expand upon those tools to learn some temporal and spatial statistical methods that are particularly helpful in environmental data science. Welcome!

Learning objectives
The goal of this course is to enable MEDS students to confidently and competently apply statistical tools to socio-environmental datasets. Essential skills and concepts are:

Summarize data numerically and graphically
Interpret random variables
Simulate data to test assumptions
Describe models using statistical notation
Draw DAGs to clarify causal relationships
Quantify uncertainty to perform inference

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Statistics is part of the scientific method
text:
Statistics is part of the scientific method

Where did lead from the Exide plant end up?
Wind carried more lead NE than SW.
Gather soil cores to measure lead concentrations across the region.
STATS STATS STATS
Interpret and communicate the results

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Two types of hypotheses


What a scientist means
Hypothesis: a testable, causal explanation for an observation

Lead emissions spread via wind.


What a statistician means
Hypothesis: a quantitative statement about a parameter of the population

The proportion of homes downwind of the plant with elevated lead levels is greater than those upwind.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Variation is natural
A statistician knows that a difference in a sample (between proportions, means, etc) is insufficient to evaluate a hypothesis.
Sampling is random!
The real question: is the difference bigger than we’d expect from sampling? Or is it consistent with sampling variation?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Variation is natural

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Assess the evidence
Given that variation is natural in sampling, how do we assess evidence?
We can’t gather new data, so we design statistical experiments based on the sample we have.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Permutation is a statistical experiment for yes/no questions
text:
Permutation is a statistical experiment for yes/no questions
Question: Is the proportion of high risk homes higher downwind than upwind?
Let’s reframe this as:
Question: If there was no relationship between lead risk and wind direction, then how often would our sample be observed?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Random to the rescue
We can simulate the “what if there’s no relationship?” scenario by randomizing the predictor variable.
Randomization breaks the link between predictor and response, but keeps all the variation from the sample.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Procedure
\(H_0\): there is no relationship/effect/etc
\(H_A\): there is a relationship/effect/etc

Calculate the observed value of the statistic (e.g., a difference in proportions)
Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic.
Repeat step 2 until the cows come home (null distribution of the statistic)
Compare the observed value to the null statistic (p-value)
Reject, or fail to reject, the null hypothesis

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Permutation visualized

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Compare the observed to the null statistic
text: Compare the observed to the null statistic

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interpret the p-value
A p-value is the probability of seeing the observed sample, if the null hypothesis is true. That’s it.
If p is less than some threshold (often 0.05 by default), then we say there is a statistically significant result. This means the sample is improbable under chance alone.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Don’t misinterpret the p-value
The following are common misconceptions:

A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true
A statistically significant result is meaningful by real-world standards
A statistically non-significant result means there’s no effect

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Permutation recap

Given only one sample, how do we estimate the natural variation of the statistic? With randomization!
Permutation breaks the connection between the predictor and response, simulating the variation of the statistic expected by chance.
Permutation yields a p-value, which says if your result is statistically significant.

You are wise enough to hold complexity.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
section: Bootstrapping is a statistical experiment for “how much?” questions
text:
Bootstrapping is a statistical experiment for “how much?” questions
Question: How much higher is the proportion of high risk homes downwind than upwind?
Let’s reframe this as:
Question: What’s the interval that we confidently think contains the population-level parameter?

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Random to the rescue

We can simulate the variation in our statistic by resampling the observations.
We’re making the critical assumption that our sample is representative of the population

Instead of getting new samples from the population (too hard!) we get “bootstrapped” samples from the sample itself.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Procedure

Calculate the observed value of the statistic (e.g., a difference in proportions)
Resample the observations with replacement and recalculate the statistic.
Repeat step 2 until the cows come home (sampling distribution)
Find the range containing a large percentage of the sampling distribution (confidence interval)

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Bootstrapping visualized

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text: Find your confidence interval

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Interpret your confidence interval
A confidence interval is a range of values that you are confident contains the population parameter.
But wait… what exactly are we confident in?
If we repeated this procedure 100 times, about 95 of those CIs would contain the population parameter.
Our confidence is in the procedure’s long-run accuracy.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Don’t misinterpret your confidence interval
The following are common misconceptions:

There’s a 95% chance the 95% CI contains the population parameter
Larger sample sizes yield more accurate confidence intervals

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Bootstrapping recap

Given only one sample, how do we estimate the natural variation of the statistic? With randomization!
Bootstrapping draws “new” samples from the original, simulating the variation of the statistic expected by sampling.
Bootstrapping yields a confidence interval, which describes a range the actual parameter probably falls in.

CIs rigorously communicate uncertainty.

title: EDS 222: Statistics for Environmental Data Science
text:
Permutation vs bootstrapping


Permutation simulates a scenario with no relationship to answer “yes/no” questions.










Bootstrapping simulates the original scenario to answer “how much?” questions.

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Between November 2013 and July 2015, contractors working under the oversight of the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) sampled soil lead concentrations at hundreds of residential properties near the former Exide Technologies battery recycling facility in Vernon, CA. Crews collected soil cores from several locations on each property and analyzed them in a laboratory for lead content. This sampling campaign, and this lab’s data, are described in the DTSC Preliminary Estimate of the Geographical Boundary of Emissions report (Department of Toxic Substances Control 2015).
A single soil sample is a measurement of a property’s soil lead level, but no single measurement perfectly captures the “true” lead burden of an entire property. In this lab you’ll explore how much soil lead measurements vary within a property, and how that variability depends on where on the property a sample was taken. This is a question about reliability: if you sampled the same property twice, how close would the two measurements be?

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Between November 2013 and July 2015, contractors working under the oversight of the California Department of Toxic Substances Control (DTSC) sampled soil lead concentrations at hundreds of residential properties near the former Exide Technologies battery recycling facility in Vernon, CA. Crews collected soil cores from several locations on each property and analyzed them in a laboratory for lead content. This sampling campaign, and this lab’s data, are described in the DTSC Preliminary Estimate of the Geographical Boundary of Emissions report (Department of Toxic Substances Control 2015).
A single soil sample is a measurement of a property’s soil lead level, but no single measurement perfectly captures the “true” lead burden of an entire property. In this lab you’ll explore how much soil lead measurements vary within a property, and how that variability depends on where on the property a sample was taken. This is a question about reliability: if you sampled the same property twice, how close would the two measurements be?

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
The data
exide-soil-cores.csv contains a subset of the DTSC’s public data table for the Exide site. You can find it on Workbench under /courses/EDS222/data. It’s limited to the samples collected during the initial and expanded assessments in 2013-2015. The full DTSC public data table contains lots more - you are encouraged to explore it further!

Data dictionary







Column
Description




property_id
Identifier for the property a sample was collected from.


sample_id
Identifier for an individual soil sample (boring).


sample_date
Date the sample was collected.


location_code
Where on the property the sample was taken. DL = drip line. YD = yard.


pb_ppm
Lead concentration, in parts per million (ppm).


longitude, latitude
Coordinates of the property (WGS84).





What does a row represent?
Each row is one soil core collected from one location on one property, at a depth of 3 inches below ground surface. Properties were sampled at multiple locations, so property_id repeats across rows: a single property typically contributes up to ten yard samples and a handful of drip line samples.


What’s a drip line?
The drip line is the narrow strip of soil at the edge of a building’s roof - the line where rainwater drips or is directed off the roof and gutters. It sits right against the house, in contrast to the rest of the yard, the more open part of the property further from the building. Because paint (a historical source of lead) tends to chip and weather off exterior walls, and because roof runoff concentrates atmospheric deposition falling on the roof into a narrow band, drip line soil can experience different pollutant exposure than yard soil.

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Lab activity

library(tidyverse)


1. Read in the data


2. Distribution of soil core lead measurements
Create a histogram to visualize the distribution of pb_ppm across all samples. How does it compare to the California (80 ppm) and EPA (200 ppm) thresholds for lead in residential soil?


3. Distribution of property-level mean measurements
Calculate the mean pb_ppm for each property. What’s the distribution of these property-level means? How does it compare to the distribution of individual soil cores from question 2?


4. Property-level variability
How variable are soil core lead measurements at the property level? Plot the distribution of property-level standard deviations of pb_ppm. What does your plot suggest about the reliability of soil lead measurements?


5. Lead measurements by location
What is the distribution of pb_ppm for drip line samples (location_code == "DL") versus everything else (the yard samples)? How much higher do drip line measurements appear to be relative to yard measurements?


6. Drip line vs. yard, at the property level
Part 5 looked at the aggregate distribution across all samples. Now let’s look at drip line vs. yard within each property.
a. Create a new column called is_dripline: a logical column that’s TRUE for drip line locations and FALSE otherwise.
b. Group the data by property and is_dripline, and calculate the mean soil lead concentration in each group.
c. For each property, calculate the difference between the mean drip line measurement and the mean non-drip-line (yard) measurement. Hint: pivoting will help!
d. Plot the distribution of the property-level drip line/yard differences.

title: Lab 1: Reliability of Soil Lead Measurements
text:
Interpretation
Interpret your final plot from the perspective of reliability. If you’re estimating the representative soil lead concentration for a property, how does sample location affect measurement reliability? What do you think you should do with the data from different locations?

These are both claims that we can investigate using statistical inference. In this week’s lab, you’ll reframe the claims using statistical language, use a statistical experiment to quantify the evidence in the sample, and interpret your results responsibly.








Claim
Question type

title: Lab 2: Foundations of Inference
text:
Investigating “yes/no” questions with permutation
Let’s investigate the claim “Lead is elevated in the drip line compared to the rest of the yard” as a yes/no question.

State your hypotheses
Recall that it is more straightforward to find evidence against a hypothesis than for it. So when we investigate yes/no questions, we set up a null hypothesis and see how much evidence there is against it.
State the null and alternative hypotheses for this claim.
\(H_0\): The difference in means is 0.
\(H_A\): The difference in means is greater than 0.


Calculate the observed value of the statistic
We’ll use the difference in means between samples from the drip line and the yard as the statistic for this question.






Important



Remember, the mean isn’t always the most appropriate statistic for representing a distribution! Always think critically about how your data relates to the question.


Calculate the difference in means between the drip line and yard observations in the sample. Remember, this should be a single number (not a data frame or pair of means).

location_summ <- soil_cores |>
  summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = location_code)

obs_diff_means <- location_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2] - location_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1]

obs_diff_means

[1] 172.9459




Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic
This statistical experiment simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) just due to chance alone. To conduct this experiment, we have to break the connection between the predictor variable (location code) and response (lead concentration). Randomizing the predictor leaves the variation in the response untouched, while removing any assocation between the two.
Shuffle the predictor variable and recalculate the statistic. Do it just once - we’ll repeat in the next section.






Tip



sample() can be used to shuffle vectors.



shuffled_summ <- soil_cores |>
  mutate(location_code = sample(location_code)) |>
  summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = location_code)

shuffled_diff_means <- shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2] -
  shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1]

shuffled_diff_means

[1] -10.1124




Repeat shuffling
In the previous section, you simulated one statistic from the null hypothesis. What we need now is a whole bunch of statistics from the null hypothesis - our null distribution.
Repeat shuffling 10,000 times to create a vector that simulates the null distribution.






Tip



replicate() repeatedly runs expressions over and over.



location_null_dist <- replicate(
  1e3,
  {
    shuffled_summ <- soil_cores |>
      mutate(location_code = sample(location_code)) |>
      summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = location_code)

    shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2] -
      shuffled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1]
  }
)

Visualize the null distribution using a histogram.

tibble(diff_means = location_null_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)














Compare the observed to the null
The previous figure showed the expected distribution of the statistic (the difference in mean lead between drip line and yard) under the null hypothesis. How does that compare to the observed value?
Plot the null distribution again, but this time add a vertical line indicating the observed statistic.

tibble(diff_means = location_null_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff_means, color = "magenta", linewidth = 1.5)












Calculate your p-value.






Note



A p-value is the probability of observing the sample (or something more extreme) if the null hypothesis is true.



pval <- mean(location_null_dist > obs_diff_means)

pval

[1] 0




Interpret your results
Based on your p-value, do you reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?

title: Lab 2: Foundations of Inference
text:
Investigating “how much?” questions with bootstrapping
Now, let’s investigate the claim “Neighborhoods north of the Exide plant were exposed to more lead than those south” as a how much? question.

Calculate the observed value of the statistic
Once again, let’s use the difference in means as our statistic. Calculate the difference in means between properties in the extended north area and those in the extended south area.






Tip



Use dplyr functions to wrangle the soil core data for this part. Properties starting with “ENA” are in the extended north area, and the “ESA” prefix means extended south area. str_sub() will help here.



ena_esa <- soil_cores |>
  mutate(area = str_sub(property_id, 1, 3)) |>
  filter(area %in% c("ENA", "ESA"))

area_summ <- ena_esa |>
  summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = area) |>
  arrange(area)

obs_diff_means <- area_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1] - area_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2]

obs_diff_means

[1] 72.45974




Resample observations and recalculate the statistic
Bootstrapping simulates the expected variation in our statistic (difference in means) from sampling. Compare this to permutation, which is about variation just due to chance. For this experiment, we will assume the sample is representative of the population and repeatedly draw “new” samples. This process simulates the process of collecting new samples.
Resample rows from the data frame and recalculate the statistic. Repeat this 10,000 times to simulate the sampling distribution.






Tip



Use slice_sample() with replacement to get bootstrap samples.



area_samp_dist <- replicate(
  1e3,
  {
    resampled_summ <- ena_esa |>
      slice_sample(n = nrow(ena_esa), replace = TRUE) |>
      summarize(mean_pb_ppm = mean(pb_ppm), .by = area) |>
      arrange(area)

    resampled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[1] -
      resampled_summ$mean_pb_ppm[2]
  }
)

Visualize the sampling distribution using a histogram.

tibble(diff_means = area_samp_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)














Find the confidence interval
The previous figure showed how your statistic varies due to slight differences between samples. Use this sampling distribution to estimate the 95% confidence interval.






Note



A confidence interval is a range of values that you are confident contains the population parameter.








Tip



Use the quantile() function to find the middle 95% of the sampling distribution.



area_95ci <- quantile(area_samp_dist, c(0.025, 0.975))

Plot the sampling distribution again, but this time add vertical lines indicating the observed statistic and the 95% CI.

tibble(diff_means = area_samp_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(diff_means)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff_means, color = "magenta", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = area_95ci, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.5)














Interpret your results
Based on your confidence interval, how much could the difference in lead exposure between north and south be?
What does this mean for your question?
What characteristics of the data may impact your inference?

More importantly, remember how to use these tools responsibly. A p-value and a confidence interval are tools for checking our own cognitive biases. They are useful lines of evidence, but no one statistical procedure ever tells the whole story.
Always think critically!
